analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and private insurers to keep covering recommended vaccines with no copays.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House in September 2025 with 83 Democratic cosponsors; referred to three House committees and has seen no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, and private and employer health plans to cover, with no out-of-pocket charge, every vaccine that the CDC's vaccine advisory committee recommended as of October 25, 2024 [S2]. It is written as a freeze: even if the advisory committee later pulls back a recommendation, plans must keep covering that vaccine at no cost to the patient through the end of 2029 [S3]. The requirements for private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP all expire on January 1, 2030 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP, and anyone covered by an employer or individual health plan. Under the bill, their vaccines stay free of copays and deductibles even if federal health officials later scale back vaccine recommendations, since plans must keep covering every vaccine on the October 2024 list through 2029 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients, Medicare and Medicaid enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP must cover all vaccines recommended by the CDC advisory committee as of October 25, 2024, with no cost sharing, through the end of 2029 [S2][S3].

If a vaccine recommendation is revoked after October 25, 2024, the bill keeps the most recent pre-revocation recommendation in force for coverage purposes, so patients do not lose free access to a vaccine they could previously get [S3].
Medicaid programs, including state benchmark plans, and the federal program that supplies free pediatric vaccines to low-income children may not drop a vaccine that was on the 2024 list [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health plans and the employers that sponsor them, along with Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP, bear the cost of covering vaccines and their administration without charging patients. In the ordinary case these costs already exist; the added cost falls if federal advisers later withdraw a recommendation that the bill keeps on the books [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and government health programs

drawbacks.text: The requirements are temporary: coverage mandates for private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP all end on January 1, 2030, after which the normal coverage rules resume [S3].

The bill locks coverage to a single date's list of recommendations rather than letting clinical guidance evolve; if a vaccine recommendation is later narrowed or revoked, plans must still cover it for patients who want it, which keeps delivering and paying for a service federal advisers no longer recommend [S3].
Coverage mandates shift vaccine costs to insurers and employer plans rather than eliminating them; any increase in required coverage can surface as higher premiums over time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to patients is real but narrow in ordinary years: most ACIP-recommended vaccines are already covered without cost-sharing under existing preventive-services rules, so the bill's main effect is protection against future rollbacks. The main cost is borne by insurers, employers, and public programs if recommendations are later withdrawn and coverage must continue anyway. The hard date of October 25, 2024 substitutes Congress's judgment for the CDC advisory process, which cuts both ways: it guarantees stability for patients but overrides subsequent clinical judgments.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce — and nothing has happened since; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the bill on September 18, 2025, joined by Reps. Richard Neal and Bobby Scott of Virginia [S1][S3].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce — for consideration of the provisions in each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
83 of 217 House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no further action is recorded [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. If the bill stays parked in committee, vaccine coverage rules remain whatever current law and federal health officials produce, so anyone who prefers that the CDC advisory process determine coverage unchanged is better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is untouched

for.what_they_did: Restructured the CDC vaccine advisory committee and changed vaccine recommendations in 2025; the bill's freeze on the October 2024 recommendation list is a direct response to that upheaval

sides.party_line_note: All 83 cosponsors are Democrats, roughly 38% of the House Democratic caucus, and no Republican cosponsor appears on the bill; with Republicans holding 223 of 441 House seats, minority-party support alone has not moved the bill out of committee.

industries.note: Insurers and employer plans must cover and waive cost-sharing for every vaccine on the October 2024 list through 2029, even if recommendations are later withdrawn, which removes their ability to stop paying for a vaccine as federal guidance narrows [S3]. For patients this is the point of the bill; for insurers it is an added obligation.

The bill guarantees a federal coverage requirement for their products through 2029 regardless of later advisory-committee changes, keeping the payer base intact. Patients keep free access, so the industry's interest in guaranteed coverage runs alongside theirs here.

States may not use benchmark plans without the no-cost-sharing vaccine benefit and must cover the full 2024 vaccine list in Medicaid and CHIP, a federal mandate that states administer — though the cost falls on a program that serves their own low-income residents [S3].

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with three committees and no scheduled hearing. Bills introduced only with minority-party support and referred to multiple committees rarely reach the floor in the same Congress; unless House leadership or a committee schedules action, the most likely path is that it remains in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress, serving as a marker for a possible future majority.
